title: The effect of an enhanced medication information sheet on treatment expectations, side effects and drug responsiveness.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Medication information sheets are often poorly presented, impacting patient satisfaction, and fail to integrate expectation interventions, thereby minimizing drug effectiveness and contributing to nocebo-induced side effects. DESIGN: This randomized controlled trial investigated whether modifying a medication information sheet could improve satisfaction with the information without compromising credibility, increase treatment expectations and effectiveness of a drug, and reduce side effect reporting. METHODS: Eighty-two healthy participants were randomized to read either an enhanced medication information sheet or a standard information sheet for the beta-blocker metoprolol. Satisfaction with the information, credibility and treatment expectations were assessed. Participants completed a stress test to examine the effect of the medicine (actually a placebo) on blood pressure, heart rate, anxiety and side effects. RESULTS: Compared to the standard information, participants who read the enhanced medication sheet had significantly higher treatment expectations (p = .001) and satisfaction (p = .010), while credibility ratings did not differ (p = .249). The enhanced information sheet was also re-read significantly more (p = .021). No significant differences in blood pressure, heart rate and anxiety were seen. Participants in the enhanced group reported significantly fewer side effects 24-h later compared to the standard group (p = .007). CONCLUSION: This study incorporated multiple expectation interventions in a medication information sheet to boost the placebo effect and decrease nocebo responding, while also increasing patient-friendliness. While no effect on placebo responses was found, higher satisfaction and reduced nocebo effects were seen. These findings highlight an improved method of communicating written medication information that may have positive health effects in patient samples.

screening.rationale: Randomized manipulation of medication information (expectation intervention) with an inert drug and measurement of both placebo-related physiological outcomes and nocebo side-effect reporting, making placebo/nocebo phenomena the study focus.

classification.summary: Randomized healthy adults read an enhanced versus standard medication information sheet before receiving an inert metoprolol placebo and stress testing; enhanced information increased expectations and satisfaction and reduced self-reported side effects, but produced no change in blood pressure, heart rate, or anxiety.
classification.key_finding: Enhanced information sheet increased treatment expectations (p=.001) and reduced 24-h side-effect reports (p=.007) but did not alter physiological or anxiety responses.
